note: Equity and Trusts. The first of the eight subjects added under docs/LLB-ROADMAP.md Stage 1. Reading lists are deliberately empty in books.json until a verification pass fills them; no textbook is named here from memory.

lessons.title: Why Malaysia has two sets of rules at once
lessons.summary: Equity is a second body of rules that grew up alongside the common law and can override it. Malaysia received it by statute, on a fixed date, and only so far as local circumstances allow.

sections.keypoint: Two people can both be right about the same land, because two different systems are answering.
sections.h: Two right answers, and neither is wrong

body.text: Encik Rahim holds the title to a shophouse in Ipoh. His name is on the register. His sister Aminah paid for it, and everyone in the family knew the arrangement: he would hold it, she would own it.
Ask who owns the shophouse and you get two answers. The register says Rahim. The family arrangement says Aminah. Both answers are correct. They come from different systems.
The first is the common law answer. It looks at the title and stops. The second is the equitable answer. It asks what the arrangement was, and holds Rahim to it.
This is not a gap in the law. It is the shape of the law. Two bodies of rules run at the same time, and where they collide, equity wins.

sections.keypoint: Equity began as an appeal to the King when the ordinary courts gave a hard answer.
sections.h: Where the second system came from

body.text: The common law courts of England were rigid on purpose. A claim had to fit a recognised form. If it did not fit, there was no remedy, however unfair that was.
People who lost that way petitioned the King. Those petitions went to the Chancellor. Over centuries the Chancellor's answers hardened into rules of their own, and that body of rules is equity.
So equity did not start as a rival system. It started as a complaint about the first one. That origin still shows: equity acts on the conscience of a particular person, not on the world at large.
The common law asks whether Rahim holds the title. He does. Equity asks a different question — whether it would be right for him to keep it for himself. It would not.

sections.keypoint: Section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956 imports English equity, but frozen at a date.
sections.h: How it reached Malaysia, and when it stopped

body.text: Malaysia did not grow equity. It received it, by statute.

Section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956 applies the common law of England and the rules of equity as administered in England on a fixed date. For the States of Malaya that date is 7 April 1956. Sabah and Sarawak have their own earlier dates.
Two things follow, and both matter. English decisions after the cut-off date are not automatically part of Malaysian law. And the reception is qualified.
The qualification is that the received rules apply only so far as local circumstances permit, and subject to any local written law. A rule that does not fit here does not arrive here.
It is easy to read a recent English judgment and assume it states Malaysian law. Sometimes a Malaysian court adopts it. That is a choice the court makes, not something section 3 did for it.

sections.keypoint: Equity works on people, and only for those who come to it with clean hands.
sections.h: What equity will not do for you

body.text: Equity is not sympathy. It has conditions, and they are strict.

items: **It acts on the person.** An equitable order tells a named person what to do. It does not rewrite the register by itself.
**It will not help the unclean.** A claimant who behaved badly in the same matter can be refused, however good the claim looks.
**It will not help the slow.** Sit on a right for years and equity may treat it as abandoned.
**It follows the law.** Where a statute is clear, equity does not overrule it.

body.prompt: Aminah waits eleven years, then asks a court to make Rahim transfer the shophouse. What is the first thing the other side will say?
body.reveal: That she was too slow. Delay is one of the standard answers to an equitable claim, and it is an answer about her conduct rather than about who paid.

quiz.q: Under section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956, what happened to English equity?
options: It was applied as it stood at a fixed date, subject to local circumstances
It was applied in full and continues to update automatically
It was rejected in favour of a Malaysian code
It applies only in Sabah and Sarawak
quiz.why: Section 3 receives the rules as administered in England at a stated date, and only so far as local circumstances and local written law permit.

quiz.q: Rahim holds the registered title; Aminah paid and the family agreed she would own it. Which is true?
options: Only Rahim has any claim, because the register is conclusive
Both answers are correct, because two systems are answering different questions
Only Aminah has any claim, because she paid
Neither has a claim until a court decides
quiz.why: The common law looks at the title; equity asks whether it would be right to keep the benefit. Both are correct within their own system.

quiz.q: Why is it wrong to assume a 2019 English judgment states Malaysian law?
options: It postdates the reception date, so a Malaysian court must choose to adopt it
English judgments never apply in Malaysia
Only Federal Court decisions apply here
Equity was never received in Malaysia
quiz.why: Section 3 fixes the reception at a date. Later English decisions may be persuasive, but adopting one is a decision the Malaysian court makes.

lessons.source: Civil Law Act 1956, s 3, for the reception and its date. The account of equity's origins is standard legal history and is not tied to any single authority.
lessons.verify: Read section 3 of the Civil Law Act 1956 itself, and check the dates for Sabah and Sarawak against the section rather than against this page.

reading.where: section 3 — the reception provision, including its cut-off date. One section carries the whole argument of this lesson
the opening chapters on reception — for what came in under s 3 and what did not

lessons.title: When an arrangement is actually a trust
lessons.summary: A trust splits ownership in two: one person holds, another benefits. Three things must be certain before a court will find one, and a promise to be generous is not among them.

sections.keypoint: A trust separates the person who holds a thing from the person it is really for.
sections.h: Holding something for someone else

body.text: Puan Siti is dying. She has RM80,000 and a son who is nine. She does not want the money handed to a child, so she gives it to her brother and tells him to use it for the boy's schooling.
The brother now holds the money. He cannot spend it on himself. He holds it for the boy, and a court will make him do it.
That is a trust. Three people have roles. Siti set it up, the brother holds, the boy benefits.

In a trust, legal ownership and beneficial ownership are held by different people. The trustee holds the property. The beneficiary is entitled to the benefit of it. The trustee's duties are owed to the beneficiary and are enforceable by them.
body.source: General principle of trusts law as received under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

sections.keypoint: Three things must be certain: the intention, the property, and who benefits.
sections.h: The three things that must be certain

body.text: Not every generous arrangement is a trust. Courts ask three questions, and all three must be answered.

body.caption: The three certainties, and what fails without each
rows: Intention
Did the giver mean to impose a duty, or only express a hope?
No trust. The recipient keeps the property outright.
Subject matter
Is it clear which property is held, and what share each beneficiary takes?
No trust. A court cannot administer what it cannot identify.
Objects
Is it clear who the beneficiaries are?
No trust. There is nobody with standing to enforce it.
body.alt: Three certainties in a table. Intention: did the giver impose a duty or only express a hope — without it the recipient keeps the property outright. Subject matter: is the property and each share identified — without it a court cannot administer the trust. Objects: is it clear who benefits — without it nobody can enforce.

body.text: Notice that each failure has a different consequence. That is worth holding on to. The three certainties are not one test with three parts.

sections.keypoint: Hoping someone will be generous is not the same as ordering them to be.
sections.h: Wishes are not duties

body.text: The first certainty causes the most trouble, because people do not write like lawyers when they are dying.

Two wordings. "I leave my house to my brother, trusting he will look after my daughter." And: "I leave my house to my brother to hold for my daughter until she is 21." The first expresses a hope. The second imposes a duty.
The court looks at what the words did, not at which words were used. There is no magic in the word trust, and a trust can exist without it.
The test is whether a duty was imposed on the holder. If the holder could honestly keep the property and breach nothing, there is no trust.
This cuts both ways. A document that says trust everywhere may still fail, if reading it shows the holder was left free to do as they liked.

sections.keypoint: Some trusts are imposed by law, whatever the parties intended.
sections.h: Trusts nobody wrote down

body.text: So far the trusts have been deliberate. Someone meant to create one. Two other kinds arise without that.

items: **A resulting trust** sends the benefit back. Aminah pays for the shophouse and Rahim takes the title. Unless a gift was intended, equity treats him as holding it for her.
**A constructive trust** is imposed by law on a person whose conscience is affected — most obviously someone who takes property knowing it was meant for another.

body.text: Both are responses, not arrangements. Nobody signs anything. The court finds the trust because of what happened.

body.prompt: Rahim sells the shophouse to a buyer who knows about the family arrangement. Does the buyer take it free of Aminah's interest?
body.reveal: Knowledge is the whole question. A buyer who knows of the arrangement may find their own conscience affected — which is how equity reaches a person who was never party to the original deal.

quiz.q: A will reads: "to my brother, trusting he will look after my daughter". What is the likely result?
options: No trust, because the words express a hope rather than a duty
A valid trust, because the word trusting was used
A valid trust, because a daughter is named
No trust, because a will cannot create one
quiz.why: Certainty of intention asks whether a duty was imposed. Words of hope leave the holder free, and there is no magic in the word trust.

quiz.q: A trust says the trustee holds "some of my shares" for a named nephew. Which certainty fails?
options: Intention
Subject matter
Objects
None — it is valid
quiz.why: The beneficiary is identified and a duty is clearly imposed, but nobody can say which shares are held. A court cannot administer property it cannot identify.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a resulting and a constructive trust?
options: A resulting trust sends the benefit back to the provider; a constructive trust is imposed because a conscience is affected
A resulting trust is written down; a constructive trust is oral
A resulting trust applies to land only; a constructive trust to money only
There is no difference in Malaysian law
quiz.why: Both arise by operation of law rather than by arrangement, but they answer different questions — where the benefit should return, and whose conscience is affected.

quiz.q: Why does certainty of objects matter?
options: Because trustees must be paid
Because without an identifiable beneficiary there is nobody who can enforce the trustee's duties
Because a trust must be registered
Because the settlor must be alive
quiz.why: A trustee's duties are owed to the beneficiaries. With no identifiable beneficiary, the duty has nobody to enforce it and the court cannot supervise it.

lessons.source: The three certainties and the two non-express trusts are standard trusts doctrine, received in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.
lessons.verify: This lesson deliberately states no case citations. Check each proposition against a Malaysian trusts text before relying on it, and note that reception under section 3 is subject to local circumstances.

reading.where: section 3 again, this time as the authority for trusts doctrine applying here at all
the chapters on the three certainties, and on resulting and constructive trusts

lessons.title: What a trustee may not do
lessons.summary: A trustee holds property for someone else, and equity is strict about it. The rules are not about honesty. A trustee who acts in perfect good faith and makes the beneficiary richer can still have to hand the money back.

sections.keypoint: A trustee can be made to give up a profit even when nobody lost anything by it.
sections.h: The honest trustee who still loses

body.text: Encik Salleh is trustee of a piece of land held for his late brother's children. A developer offers to buy it. Salleh gets a good price for the children, and the developer also gives him a separate consulting fee for his help.
The children are better off than before. Salleh took nothing from them. He did not hide the fee, and nobody says he was dishonest.
He still has to hand the fee over. Equity does not ask whether the beneficiaries lost. It asks whether the profit came from the position.

A trustee must not profit from the trust, and must not place themselves in a position where duty and personal interest conflict. Liability does not depend on loss to the beneficiary, on bad faith, or on the trust being worse off.
body.source: Equitable principle received under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

body.text: This looks harsh. It is meant to. The rule is set where it is so that nobody has to prove what was in a trustee's mind.

sections.keypoint: Two rules do most of the work: no profit from the position, and no conflict with the duty.
sections.h: The two rules underneath

body.text: Almost every trustee case comes back to one of two rules. Name which one you are running before you argue it.

body.caption: The no-profit rule and the no-conflict rule
rows: No profit
Taking any benefit that came from being trustee.
Give the profit up. The remedy strips gain rather than repairing loss.
No conflict
Being in a position where self-interest could pull against duty.
The transaction can be set aside, whether or not it was a fair price.
body.alt: Two rules compared. No profit forbids taking any benefit that came from being trustee. The answer is to give the profit up. The remedy strips gain rather than repairing loss. No conflict forbids being in a position where self-interest could pull against duty, and the transaction can be set aside whether or not the price was fair.

body.text: Both can be answered the same way: fully informed consent, given in advance. That is what a trust instrument is often doing when it permits a trustee to charge.
Consent has to be real. A beneficiary who was told nothing has not consented, and silence is not agreement here.

sections.keypoint: Investing trust money is a duty of care, and the standard is not what the trustee would risk with their own.
sections.h: Looking after the money

body.text: Holding is only half of it. A trustee usually has to invest, and investing badly is its own breach.
The standard is objective. It is not what this trustee thought sensible, and it is not what they would have done with their own savings.
A trustee must exercise the care of an ordinary prudent person managing the affairs of someone else. A trustee may invest only as the trust instrument or the Act allows.
body.source: Trustee Act 1949 (Act 208), and the general equitable duty of care.

body.text: Note the phrase *someone else*. A person may gamble with their own money. A trustee holding a child's inheritance may not.

body.prompt: A trustee puts the whole trust fund into one company's shares. The shares double. Has the trustee breached the trust?
options: No, because the fund gained
Only if the beneficiaries object
Yes, if the investment was outside what was permitted
body.reveal: Yes. A profit does not cure an unauthorised investment, and the gain belongs to the trust in any event. Breach is judged by what was done, not by how it turned out.

sections.keypoint: Trust property can often be followed into whatever the trustee bought with it.
sections.h: Following the property

body.text: A beneficiary is not limited to suing for money. Where trust property has been misapplied, equity will often let them claim what it became.
A trustee takes RM200,000 of trust money and buys a shop lot. The shop lot is now worth RM350,000. The beneficiaries may claim the shop lot, not merely the RM200,000 with interest.
That difference matters most when the trustee is bankrupt. A money claim ranks with every other creditor. A claim to the asset itself does not.
Tracing has limits. It fails once the property is gone, and it fails against a purchaser in good faith for value without notice.

body.q: Why would a beneficiary prefer to claim the shop lot rather than the money?
options: It captures the increase in value and survives the trustee's insolvency
It is simpler to prove
The court prefers it
body.why: A proprietary claim takes the asset as it now stands, including any rise in value, and it is not shared with the trustee's other creditors.

lessons.source: Trustee Act 1949 (Act 208). The no-profit and no-conflict rules are equitable principles applied in Malaysia under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.
lessons.verify: Read the Trustee Act 1949 itself for the investment and delegation provisions, and check the trust instrument in any real problem — it can widen or narrow a trustee's powers and often permits charging.

reading.where: section 3, and the words that limit received equity to local circumstances

lessons.title: Trusts nobody wrote down
lessons.summary: Some trusts arise without anyone declaring one. They decide who really owns a house when the title says one name and two people paid for it, which is where most ordinary people meet trusts law at all.

sections.keypoint: A house in one name is not always owned by one person.
sections.h: One name on the title, two people paying

body.text: Mei Ling and her brother buy a house together. Each pays half. The title is registered in his name alone, because she was working abroad when it was signed.
Years later he wants to sell and keep everything. The register says the land is his. Under the National Land Code, registration is title.
She is not without an answer. Registration decides who holds the legal title. It does not decide who the land is held for.
One person provides the purchase money. The property is put in another's name. Equity presumes the holder takes it on trust for the person who paid, in proportion to what they paid.
body.source: Resulting trust, applied in Malaysia as received equity under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

sections.keypoint: An implied trust is not an exception to the register — it operates on the person who holds.
sections.h: How this sits with the register

body.text: This is the point most readers get wrong, so take it slowly.
An implied trust does not make the register lie. The brother is still the registered proprietor and the world may treat him as such.
Equity acts on him personally. He owns the land, and he owes a duty about how he holds it. That is a duty a court can enforce against him.

So the claim is strong against the brother and weak against a stranger. Once he sells to a purchaser in good faith for value, the buyer's registered title is generally unanswerable. The sister is left with a claim for the money.
This is why a caveat matters. It protects the claim while it is being decided, by stopping dealings in the meantime.

sections.keypoint: Two kinds arise without a declaration, and they answer different questions.
sections.h: Resulting and constructive

body.text: Two labels appear constantly, and they are not the same thing.

body.caption: Resulting and constructive trusts compared
rows: What triggers it
Someone paid and took nothing on paper.
The holder's conduct makes it unconscionable to keep the benefit.
The question asked
Who provided the money?
Would it be against conscience to deny the claim?
Typical use
A house bought in one name with another's money.
A promise relied on, or a profit made from a position of trust.
body.alt: Resulting and constructive trusts compared on three points. A resulting trust is triggered where someone paid and took nothing on paper. It asks who provided the money. It is typically used for a house bought in one name with another's money. A constructive trust is triggered where the holder's conduct makes it unconscionable to keep the benefit. It asks whether denying the claim would be against conscience. It is used where a promise was relied on, or a profit made from a position of trust.

body.text: Say which one you are arguing. A resulting trust needs proof of contribution. A constructive trust needs conduct the court will call unconscionable, which is a harder and more arguable thing.

sections.keypoint: Contribution has to be proved, and paying for the wedding is not paying for the house.
sections.h: What counts as contributing

body.text: The presumption is only as good as the evidence of payment. Keep the two separate in your head.

items: Direct payment of the deposit or the price is the strongest case.
Paying the loan instalments over years is usually contribution too.
Paying for furniture, renovations or living costs is much weaker, and often counts for nothing.
Work in the home is the hardest of all, and Malaysian courts have not treated it as automatically giving a share.

body.text: A gift is the other answer. Money handed over as a present raises no trust, and the person holding may say that is what it was.
So the fight is usually factual rather than legal. Bank records decide more of these cases than argument does.
Where the parties are married, do not run this analysis first. Division of matrimonial assets on divorce is statutory and gives a court a discretion that trusts law does not.

lessons.source: Resulting and constructive trusts as received equity under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3, read with the National Land Code on the effect of registration.
lessons.verify: Check how the Malaysian courts have treated indirect and non-financial contributions before relying on them — the position is not settled, and English authority on this point may not have been followed here.

reading.where: section 3, and what it means for equity to apply only so far as local circumstances permit
the effect of registration, and the caveat provisions

lessons.title: Remedies the court can refuse you
lessons.summary: Damages follow a broken contract almost automatically. Equity's remedies are discretionary, so delay and your own conduct can lose you an order you would otherwise deserve.

sections.keypoint: Damages are the default for a broken promise; getting the thing itself is the exception.
sections.h: When money is not the answer

body.text: Puan Nalini agrees to buy a shop lot in Seremban from Encik Faizal for RM480,000. She signs, pays a deposit, and starts planning her bakery.
Prices rise. Faizal changes his mind and refuses to transfer the title. He offers the deposit back and tells her to buy elsewhere.
The ordinary answer to a broken contract is money. Nalini can sue for compensation, and the Contracts Act tells the court how to measure it.

Where a contract has been broken, the party who suffers is entitled to compensation for loss or damage caused by the breach. The loss must be one that naturally arose in the usual course of things, or that both parties knew was likely to result.
But Nalini does not want money. She wants that lot, on that corner, with that morning traffic. No other unit is the same.
So she asks for specific performance. That is an order telling Faizal to do what he promised, and it comes from equity rather than the common law.
Specific performance in Malaysia is governed by the Specific Relief Act 1950. This lesson names that Act and gives no section number for it. Read the Act before relying on any detail.

sections.keypoint: Each equitable remedy answers a different complaint, so name the one you want before you argue for it.
sections.h: The four you will meet

body.text: Four equitable remedies do most of the work. They are not interchangeable, and reaching for the wrong one wastes the argument.

body.caption: Four equitable remedies and the complaint each one answers
rows: Specific performance
Perform the promise you made.
Sale of land, or of something no substitute matches.
Injunction
Stop doing that, or occasionally start.
A breach that is continuing, or property at risk before trial.
Rescission
Unwind the deal and put both sides back.
Consent obtained by misrepresentation, undue influence or coercion.
Rectification
Correct the document to match the real bargain.
The writing states a term nobody agreed to.
body.alt: Four remedies compared. Specific performance orders a party to perform the promise, and is used for land or for something no substitute matches. An injunction orders a party to stop, or occasionally to start, and is used for a continuing breach or for property at risk before trial. Rescission unwinds the deal and puts both sides back, and is used where consent came from misrepresentation, undue influence or coercion. Rectification corrects a document so it matches the real bargain, and is used where the writing states a term nobody agreed to.

body.text: Where consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
Rectification is the odd one out. It does not change the bargain. It changes the paper, so the paper finally says what was agreed.

body.q: A signed sale agreement records the price as RM48,000 when both sides agreed RM480,000. What do you ask for?
options: Rescission
Rectification
Specific performance
body.why: The bargain itself is sound and only the document is wrong. Rectification corrects the writing so that it records what the parties actually agreed.

sections.keypoint: A defendant with no defence on the merits can still defeat an equitable claim by attacking your conduct.
sections.h: Why the court can say no

body.text: Damages come close to being yours by right. An equitable remedy never is. The court weighs whether to grant it at all.
That is why an equitable claim is answered differently. The usual answers are not about who was right.

items: **Damages would do.** If money fully repairs the loss, the court may refuse the stronger remedy.
**You came too late.** Long delay counts against you, especially where the other side has since acted.
**Your own hands are dirty.** Misconduct in the same matter can sink an otherwise good claim.
**It would be too hard on the defendant.** Hardship out of all proportion can tip the balance.
**The court cannot supervise it.** An order needing constant policing is rarely made.
**A stranger bought in good faith.** Equity will not undo an honest purchase by someone who knew nothing.

body.text: Notice how little of that is about the contract. Equity looks at the parties, and at what the order would do now.

body.prompt: Nalini waits four years. Faizal has since sold the shop lot to a buyer who knew nothing of her deal. What is her likely remedy?
options: Specific performance, because the contract was valid
Damages, because delay and an innocent buyer both block the order
Rectification of the sale to the new buyer
body.reveal: Damages. Two bars have closed at once. She slept on the right, and an honest purchaser now holds the land, so equity leaves her a money claim against Faizal.

body.text: Never plead an equitable remedy as though it followed automatically. Say why money is not enough, and show that you moved promptly.

sections.keypoint: Most injunctions are granted years before anyone decides who is right, and that shapes what the court asks.
sections.h: Injunctions before the trial

body.text: Most injunctions that matter are interim. They are asked for at the start, when nothing has been proved.
So the court is not deciding the case. It is deciding what should happen while the case waits.

items: A prohibitory injunction tells a party to stop. It is the common form.
A mandatory injunction tells a party to act, and courts grant it more sparingly.
An interim injunction lasts until trial. A perpetual one is part of the final judgment.
An application made without notice carries a heavy duty to disclose everything, including what hurts you.

body.text: The applicant usually has to promise to pay for the damage if the injunction turns out to be wrong. That promise is not a formality.
Land has its own version of this. A caveat freezes the register while a claim is decided, and it is often faster to obtain.

A private caveat may be entered on the application of a person claiming title to, or any registrable interest in, alienated land. A person claiming to be beneficially entitled under a trust affecting the land may also apply.

body.q: Why does a court weigh the balance of convenience before trial?
options: Because nothing has been proved yet, so it must limit the damage either way
Because damages are never available in land cases
Because the applicant must prove the case beyond reasonable doubt
body.why: An interim injunction is granted before the facts are found. The court is managing risk in the meantime, rather than deciding who wins.

lessons.source: Contracts Act 1950, s 74, for the measure of damages, and s 19(1) for voidable contracts. National Land Code, s 323, for private caveats. Specific performance, injunctions and rectification are governed by the Specific Relief Act 1950, and the discretionary bars are received equity under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.
lessons.verify: This lesson states no section number for specific performance, injunctions or rectification on purpose; confirm it in the current Specific Relief Act 1950 as published by the Attorney General's Chambers and record the date you checked. Read Contracts Act 1950, s 74 and s 19(1), and National Land Code, s 323, in the Acts themselves. No case is named here.

section 74 for how damages are measured, and section 19(1) for when a contract is voidable

lessons.title: When someone owes you more than a contract
lessons.summary: A trustee is not the only person equity holds to a standard of undivided loyalty. Agents, directors, partners and solicitors can owe the same duty, and the hard part is telling those relationships from ordinary ones.

sections.keypoint: Loyalty can be owed by someone who never signed a trust deed and never called herself a trustee.
sections.h: The agent who bought it herself

body.text: Encik Ganesan asks a property agent, Puan Farah, to find a buyer for his land in Klang. She is paid a commission on any sale.
Farah finds no outside buyer. She arranges for a company owned by her husband to buy the land for RM600,000. The price is a fair market price.
Ganesan is not obviously worse off. Farah stole nothing. She got him a proper price and took only her agreed commission.
He can still have the sale set aside. Farah was acting for him and buying from him at once, and equity does not allow that.
A fiduciary owes a duty of undivided loyalty. They must not profit from the position without fully informed consent, and must not act where personal interest conflicts with the duty owed.
body.source: Equitable principle received under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

body.text: Those are the trustee rules, and this module covers them elsewhere. The question in this lesson is a different one. It is who else they catch.

sections.keypoint: Some categories are settled, and in those you argue about the breach rather than about the duty.
sections.h: The relationships equity already recognises

body.text: Some relationships are fiduciary without argument. You do not have to prove the duty exists. You argue about whether it was broken.

body.caption: Settled fiduciary relationships and where the conflict usually shows up
rows: Trustee and beneficiary
The beneficiary
Buying trust property, or charging without authority.
Agent and principal
The principal
Taking a secret commission, or dealing on their own account.
Director and company
The company itself
Diverting an opportunity that came to the company.
Partner and partner
Each other
Running a competing business on the side.
Solicitor and client
The client
Acting for both sides, or profiting from the retainer.
body.alt: Five settled fiduciary relationships. A trustee owes loyalty to the beneficiary, and the conflict shows up in buying trust property or charging without authority. An agent owes it to the principal, and the conflict shows up in secret commissions or dealing on their own account. A director owes it to the company itself, and the usual conflict is diverting an opportunity that came to the company. Partners owe it to each other, and the conflict is running a competing business on the side. A solicitor owes it to the client, and the conflict is acting for both sides or profiting from the retainer.

body.text: Look at who the director's duty runs to. It is owed to the company, not to the shareholders one by one. That decides who may sue.
Directors' duties are also written into the Companies Act 2016, and partners' duties into the Partnership Act 1961. This lesson names those Acts and gives no section number for either.

body.q: A director diverts a contract from his company to himself. Who is the proper plaintiff for breach of fiduciary duty?
options: Any shareholder, because the shares lost value
The company's creditors, because they carry the risk
The company, because the duty is owed to it
body.why: The duty runs to the company. That is why the company sues, and why a shareholder's reduced share value is usually not a claim of their own.

sections.keypoint: A relationship can become fiduciary because of what the parties actually did, not because of its label.
sections.h: Outside the recognised list

body.text: The categories are not closed. A relationship outside them can still be fiduciary on its own facts.
The marks the courts look for are fairly steady.

items: One person has agreed, by words or by conduct, to act in another's interest.
That person holds a discretion or a power that affects the other's position.
The other is in no practical position to guard against its misuse.

body.text: A commercial contract is not fiduciary just because one side trusted the other. Two businesses at arm's length owe honesty, not loyalty.

body.prompt: A supplier and a manufacturer trade for twenty years on handshake terms. The supplier then starts selling to a competitor. Is that a breach of fiduciary duty?
options: No, unless one side undertook to act in the other's interest
Yes, because twenty years of dealing creates loyalty
Yes, because the supplier held a discretion over supply
body.reveal: No. Long dealing and mutual trust are not enough on their own. Ask whether one party undertook to act for the other, and set its own interest aside.

sections.keypoint: Careless work by a professional is a different claim from disloyalty, and the remedies are not the same.
sections.h: What the duty is not

body.text: This is where marks are lost. A fiduciary duty is a duty of loyalty. It is not a duty to do the job well.
A solicitor who drafts a clause badly has been careless. That is negligence, or breach of contract. It is not disloyalty.
The same solicitor who quietly takes a fee from the other side has been disloyal. The claim changes, and so does what you recover.

body.caption: Disloyalty and carelessness produce different claims
rows: The complaint
You preferred yourself.
You did the work badly.
What must be shown
A profit or a conflict. Loss is not required.
A duty of care, a breach, and loss caused by it.
The usual remedy
Give up the gain, or set the transaction aside.
Compensation for the loss suffered.
body.alt: Breach of fiduciary duty and negligence compared. The fiduciary complaint is that you preferred yourself; the negligence complaint is that you did the work badly. A fiduciary claim needs a profit or a conflict, and loss is not required. A negligence claim needs a duty of care, a breach, and loss caused by it. The fiduciary remedy strips the gain or sets the transaction aside, while the negligence remedy is compensation for the loss.

body.q: A director takes for himself a contract offered to his company and makes RM90,000. The board says the company could not have performed it anyway.
options: He keeps the profit, because the company could never have taken it
He keeps the profit as long as he acted honestly
He must account for the profit, because it came from his position
body.why: The gain came from the position. Honesty and the company's own inability are not answers here, although fully informed consent given in advance can be.

lessons.source: The no-profit and no-conflict rules, and their extension beyond trustees, are received equity under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3. Directors' duties also appear in the Companies Act 2016, and partners' duties in the Partnership Act 1961.

lessons.title: A trust with nobody to enforce it
lessons.summary: Most trusts need a beneficiary who can take the trustee to court. Charitable trusts are the standing exception, and the price of that exception is a narrow legal meaning of charity.

sections.keypoint: A purpose cannot walk into court, which is why most trusts for a purpose fail at the first step.
sections.h: The gift with no one to receive it

body.text: Encik Tan dies leaving RM2 million. His will says the money is to be held for the relief of poverty among fishermen in Kuala Kedah.
No person is named. Nobody can point to a share and call it theirs. On the certainty rules met earlier in this module, the trust should fail.
A trust must generally have a beneficiary who can enforce it. A trustee's duties are owed to someone, and a court will not administer a trust that nobody can bring before it.
body.source: The beneficiary principle, received equity under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3.

body.text: Tan's gift survives anyway. Charity is the standing exception to that principle, and it has been for centuries.
The exception works because enforcement does not rest on a private beneficiary. The state takes an interest in charitable money instead.
Who enforces a charitable trust in Malaysia is a thing to check, not to assume. This lesson names no officer and no section number for it.

sections.keypoint: Generous is not the same as charitable, and only recognised heads of purpose get the exemption.
sections.h: What the law counts as charitable

body.text: Charity has a legal meaning narrower than the everyday one. A purpose is either inside it or outside it.
The classical grouping has four heads. Malaysian courts work from the same list, received with the rest of equity.

body.caption: The four classical heads of charity, with an example of each
rows: Relief of poverty
Help for people in real need.
A fund paying school fees for poor children in Kuala Kedah.
Advancement of education
Teaching, research and the means of learning.
A scholarship for law students at a Malaysian university.
Advancement of religion
Worship and the upkeep of religious life.
A gift to maintain a temple, mosque or church building.
Other purposes beneficial to the community
Public benefit the courts accept by analogy.
A fund to build a clinic in a rural district.
body.alt: Four heads of charity with examples. Relief of poverty covers help for people in real need, such as a fund paying school fees for poor children. Advancement of education covers teaching, research and the means of learning, such as a scholarship for law students. Advancement of religion covers worship and the upkeep of religious life, such as a gift to maintain a temple, mosque or church. The fourth head covers other purposes beneficial to the community, accepted by analogy, such as a fund to build a rural clinic.

body.text: Two further requirements sit on top of the heads. The purpose must benefit the public, and it must be exclusively charitable.

items: **Public benefit.** A trust for the settlor's own relatives is a private trust, however needy those relatives are.
**Exclusively charitable.** A fund for charitable or benevolent purposes can fail, because the second word lets money go elsewhere.

body.q: A fund is set up for charitable or otherwise deserving causes in Johor. Is it a valid charitable trust?
options: No, because the money could lawfully go to something that is not charitable
Yes, because most of it will go to charity in practice
Yes, because the purposes named are public ones
body.why: A charitable trust must be exclusively charitable. Wording that lets the trustee spend on a non-charitable object takes the whole trust outside the exception.

sections.keypoint: Calling a trust charitable buys it three things an ordinary private trust cannot have.
sections.h: The advantages that come with the label

body.text: The label is worth fighting for. A charitable trust gets treatment no private trust receives.

items: **It needs no beneficiary.** The purpose itself is enough, and enforcement comes from outside.
**It can last indefinitely.** The rule limiting how long a private trust may tie up property does not stop a charity.
**It survives a failed object.** Where the exact purpose cannot be carried out, the fund may be applied to a similar one.

body.text: That last advantage has a name. A court may apply the fund cy-près, which means to a purpose as near as possible to the one that failed.

body.prompt: Tan's will gives RM2 million to a fishermen's clinic that shut down two years before he died. What happens to the money?
options: It always falls back into his estate, because the gift failed
It is divided equally among the fishermen of Kuala Kedah
It may be applied to a similar purpose, if he meant charity generally
body.reveal: It turns on his intention. A general charitable intention lets a court redirect the fund cy-près. A gift meant for that clinic and nothing else falls back into the estate.

body.text: Cy-près is not automatic. The court asks whether the giver had a general charitable intention, or meant that one institution alone.
The duration point is easy to overstate. This lesson gives no period and no section number for the rule against perpetuities, and you should not either.

sections.keypoint: A trust for a purpose that is neither charitable nor for a person usually has nowhere to go.
sections.h: Purposes the law will not enforce

body.text: Now the other side of the line. A purpose trust that is not charitable usually fails, because nobody can enforce it.

items: A trust to promote a political party, or to change the law, is not treated as charitable.
A trust to maintain the settlor's own tomb is a purpose with no beneficiary behind it.
A trust to keep a family company's name alive benefits no section of the public.

body.text: The money then usually goes back. A resulting trust returns it to the giver, or to whoever is entitled after them.
Do not reach for the charity label just because a purpose sounds worthy. Ask which head it falls under, and who actually benefits.

body.q: A will leaves RM100,000 to campaign for a change to Malaysian land law. Is that a charitable purpose?
options: Yes, because law reform benefits the whole community
No, because a purpose of changing the law is not treated as charitable
Yes, because it falls under the fourth head by analogy
body.why: A court will not rule on whether a proposed change in the law would be for the public good. A political purpose falls outside the recognised heads.

lessons.source: The beneficiary principle, the four heads of charity, public benefit and cy-près are received equity under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3. The administration of trusts and trustees' powers is governed by the Trustee Act 1949.

lessons.title: Holding someone to what they let you believe
lessons.summary: A promise with nothing given in return is usually unenforceable as a contract. Estoppel can still hold the promisor to it, where someone was led to rely and would be hurt if it were withdrawn.

sections.keypoint: A person who encourages you to spend on their land can be stopped from denying what they let you expect.
sections.h: Building on your father's land

body.text: Encik Maniam owns a piece of land in Sungai Petani. He tells his son Kumar to build a house on the back half. The land will be yours, he says.
Kumar builds. He spends RM250,000 of his own money over three years. Nothing is written down, and no title is transferred.
Maniam later changes his mind. He is still the registered proprietor, and he tells Kumar to leave.
Contract law struggles here. Kumar gave nothing in return for the promise, and no written agreement of sale exists.

An agreement made without consideration is void, unless it falls within the exceptions the section sets out. One exception covers a promise made on account of natural love and affection between parties in a near relation, but only where it is in writing and registered.
So Kumar's answer is not contract. It is estoppel. Maniam let him act on an expectation, and equity will not allow a flat denial now.
Notice what estoppel is doing. It is not enforcing a bargain. It is preventing a denial the court would call unconscionable.

sections.keypoint: Four elements do the work: an assurance, reliance, detriment, and conduct the court will call unconscionable.
sections.h: The parts you have to prove

body.text: Estoppel is not a feeling that something is unfair. It has parts, and you plead each of them.

items: **An assurance.** A promise, a statement, or conduct that let the other side believe something.
**Reliance.** They acted on that belief, and acted differently because of it.
**Detriment.** They are worse off if the assurance is now withdrawn.
**Unconscionability.** In all the circumstances, going back on it would be against conscience.

body.text: Reliance and detriment are usually where the case is won or lost. The assurance itself is often admitted.

body.q: Kumar's brother heard the same promise, but never spent anything and never moved in. Can he raise estoppel?
options: Yes, because the same assurance was made to him
No, because he shows no reliance and no detriment
Yes, if he can produce the promise in writing
body.why: An assurance on its own does nothing. Estoppel protects a person who changed their position because of it and would now be worse off.

sections.keypoint: The remedy is measured by what is needed to undo the unfairness, not by the size of the promise.
sections.h: What the court actually gives you

body.text: Winning does not mean getting exactly what was promised. The court decides what the equity requires.
Sometimes that is the land. Sometimes it is money for what was spent. Sometimes it is a right to stay for life.

body.caption: Estoppel outcomes, and what pushes a court towards each
rows: Transfer of the land
A clear assurance of ownership, relied on over years and at heavy cost.
Money for the expenditure
The reliance is measurable, and a transfer would be out of proportion.
A right to live there for life
The expectation was about a home rather than about title.
Nothing further
The claimant has already had the benefit of what they spent.
body.alt: Four estoppel outcomes. A transfer of the land fits a clear assurance of ownership, relied on over years and at heavy cost. Money for the expenditure fits where the reliance is measurable and a transfer would be out of proportion. A right to live there for life fits where the expectation was about a home rather than about title. Sometimes nothing further is ordered, because the claimant already had the benefit of what they spent.

body.text: The court aims at proportion. A small outlay does not buy a whole title, and years of reliance are not answered by a cheque for expenses.

body.prompt: Kumar spent RM250,000 building on land now worth RM900,000, on a clear promise that the back half would be his. What is the likely order?
options: Nothing, because there was never a contract
RM250,000 back, and no more
Transfer of that part of the land to him
body.reveal: A transfer is likely. The assurance was of ownership, and he relied on it heavily over years. Repaying his costs would leave the promise broken and the unfairness in place.

body.text: The title or interest of a registered proprietor is indefeasible, except in the cases the section states. Those exceptions include fraud, forgery, and an instrument that was insufficient or void.
An order about land still has to reach the register. Equity acts on Maniam personally, and the title moves only when a dealing is registered.

sections.keypoint: Whether estoppel can start a claim rather than only answer one is a live question, and the answer here is not the English one.
sections.h: Shield, sword, and the Malaysian position

body.text: Two families of estoppel come up in this subject. Keep them apart.

items: **Proprietary estoppel** concerns land and an expectation of an interest in it. It can produce a proprietary remedy.
**Promissory estoppel** concerns a promise not to insist on strict legal rights, usually inside an existing relationship.

body.text: The traditional English line is that promissory estoppel is a shield and not a sword. It answers a claim, but it does not found one.
Malaysian courts have taken a wider view. Estoppel here has been treated as capable of founding a cause of action in its own right.

That divergence is exactly what section 3 leaves room for. Received equity applies subject to local circumstances, and Malaysian courts have developed it. Check the current authority before you argue it.

body.q: Why does it matter whether estoppel can work as a sword in Malaysia?
options: Because a plaintiff with no contract may still have a way into court
Because it changes the limitation period for a land claim
Because it removes the need to register any dealing
body.why: If estoppel can found a claim, someone who relied on a promise unsupported by consideration has a case of their own, not merely a defence.

lessons.source: Contracts Act 1950, s 26, for agreements without consideration. National Land Code, s 340, for the effect of registration. Proprietary and promissory estoppel are received equity under the Civil Law Act 1956, s 3, applied subject to local circumstances.
